notes: All Phase 1 resistance sessions begin with a 5-minute treadmill or bike warm-up followed by dynamic mobility (leg swings, hip circles, arm circles, bodyweight squats).
Phase 2 MetCon session begins with 5 minutes light cardio followed by 4 × 20-second progressive efforts building from 60% to 80% effort before the interval block.
Phase 3 MetCon session begins with 8 minutes easy cycling and dynamic mobility followed by 4 × 20-second progressive efforts building to 85% effort.
Phase 3 Session 1 (Lower Body) begins with a 12-minute warm-up including assault bike, banded activation, bodyweight squats, and barbell squat warm-up sets before primary compound work.
Phase 3 Session 2 (Upper Body) begins with a 10-minute warm-up including rowing machine, band pull-aparts, face pulls, and bench press warm-up sets before primary compound work.
Phase 3 Session 5 (Saturday Power) begins with a 10-minute warm-up including assault bike, dynamic mobility, medicine ball slam warm-up, and jump squat warm-up before power blocks.
Phase 3 MetCon Block 3 (lactate flush, 7 minutes at 60–65% max HR) is explicitly labelled 'do not skip'.
Week 4 deload is described as mandatory — 'do not skip the deload'.
Phase 2 Week 7 introduces antagonist supersets on all accessory exercises (bicep curls paired with tricep pushdowns; lateral raises paired with face pulls).
Phase 3 every session ends with a timed metabolic finisher (6–12 minutes AMRAP) to maximise EPOC and post-exercise insulin sensitivity.

Fasted morning cardio sessions are strictly governed by blood glucose monitoring protocols — check blood glucose before starting; if below 5.5 mmol/L consume 15g low-GI carbohydrate and wait 15 minutes before beginning.
Phase 2 sessions on Tuesday and Thursday require a minimum 4-hour gap between fasted morning cardio and the afternoon resistance session.
Phase 3 sessions on Tuesday and Thursday require a minimum 4-hour gap between fasted morning cardio and the afternoon resistance session.
Phase 3 Thursday session uses giant sets (four exercises consecutively with no rest between exercises within each set).
Peak training weeks are identified as Weeks 10 and 11.
Intermittent fasting 12:12 introduced in Week 5 if client is ready; progressed to 14:10 in Week 6 if 12:12 well-tolerated.
Week 8 deload reduces to 3 sessions (one upper, one lower, one light cardio) and drops sets by one per exercise while maintaining loads.
Phase 3 cluster sets use 15–20 second intra-set rest periods between rep clusters.
Phase 3 rest-pause sets: perform set to near-failure, rest 15 seconds, perform additional reps, rest 15 seconds, perform final cluster.
Phase 3 drop sets: after final working set immediately reduce load by 25–30% and perform AMRAP.
Power training in Phase 3 prescribes maximum speed intent on the concentric phase of compound movements.
Cool-down after Phase 3 Session 1 is 8 minutes including pigeon pose, hamstring stretch, hip flexor stretch, quad stretch, and child's pose.
Phase 3 Session 3 cool-down is 5 minutes full static stretching.

notes: Post-workout snack context varies by session type: fasted morning cardio (Scenario A), afternoon/evening resistance session (Scenario B), or conditioning/circuit session (Scenario C).
Scenario A (post-fasted cardio): most urgent recovery window; needs protein and moderate low-GI carbohydrate promptly.
Scenario B (post-afternoon/evening resistance): bridges gap to next full meal; prioritises protein and small carbohydrate component.
Scenario C (post-conditioning/circuit): slightly more carbohydrate appropriate due to higher energy expenditure.
Minimum 15g protein per snack is a non-negotiable parameter.
Low to moderate GI carbohydrates only.
No added sugar or minimal added sugar.
Hard-boiled eggs (2) provide only 12g protein, below the ideal 15–20g threshold; pairing with cottage cheese, oatcakes, or edamame is recommended.
Roasted chickpeas alone are insufficient as a standalone post-workout snack; must be paired with a protein source.
Kefir protein content (8g) is too low to serve as a standalone post-workout snack; recommended as supplementary or paired option.
For Scenario C (post-conditioning), add a small banana to whey protein shake to bring carbohydrate content to 25–30g.
If using a protein shake immediately post-session, a proper meal should still be consumed within 60–90 minutes.
Post-workout window for fasted morning sessions: eating promptly is important for blood glucose stabilisation and muscle protection.
Post-workout window for afternoon resistance sessions: slightly more relaxed, 30–60 minutes before next meal.
Blood glucose should be checked after the session before consuming the snack, particularly in early weeks.
If post-session blood glucose is above 8.0 mmol/L, favour lower-carbohydrate options (Greek yoghurt, eggs, protein shake, edamame) and skip oatcakes or other carbohydrate additions.
If post-session blood glucose is below 5.5 mmol/L, prioritise options with moderate carbohydrate component (cottage cheese and oatcakes, tuna and oatcakes) and consume promptly.
Trainer recommendation: prepare a weekly snack box at the start of each week (batch-boil eggs, portion oatcakes, buy multipacks of yoghurt and tuna pouches — approximately 15 minutes on a Sunday).
Plain rice cakes have a relatively high GI (approximately 82), but protein and fat from salmon and cream cheese significantly blunt the glucose response when eaten together.
Chickpeas have a very low GI (approximately 28) due to high fibre and resistant starch content.

# 12-Week Training & Nutrition Programme
## Client Profile Summary
**Age:** 45 | **Condition:** Type 2 Diabetes (Metformin) | **HbA1c:** 7.2% | **Goals:** Fat loss, glycaemic control improvement | **Setting:** Full gym access

---

> **⚠️ Clinical Note for Trainer**
> Before commencing, confirm the following with the client's GP or diabetes care team: clearance for moderate-to-vigorous exercise, baseline blood glucose monitoring protocol, and whether hypoglycaemia risk is relevant (Metformin alone carries low hypo risk, but confirm no other medications). Advise client to monitor blood glucose before and after sessions, particularly in the first four weeks. Keep fast-acting glucose (e.g., glucose tablets or juice) accessible during sessions as a precaution. Any HbA1c changes should be reviewed with her medical team at the 6-week and 12-week marks.

---

## Programme Philosophy

The programme is built around three evidence-based pillars for type 2 diabetes management and fat loss:

1. **Resistance training as the primary driver** — skeletal muscle is the largest site of glucose disposal. Building and maintaining muscle mass directly improves insulin sensitivity and glycaemic control.
2. **Strategic cardiovascular work** — moderate-intensity steady-state and interval-based cardio improve mitochondrial density, cardiovascular health, and caloric expenditure without excessive cortisol stress.
3. **Nutritional precision** — carbohydrate timing and quality are managed around training to blunt post-meal glucose spikes, support performance, and create a sustainable caloric deficit for fat loss.

The 12 weeks are divided into three four-week phases, each progressively increasing in intensity and complexity.

---

## Phases at a Glance

| Phase | Weeks | Focus | Training Days/Week |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — Foundation | 1–4 | Movement quality, metabolic baseline, habit formation | 4 |
| 2 — Development | 5–8 | Progressive overload, increased intensity, metabolic conditioning | 5 |
| 3 — Intensification | 9–12 | Strength-endurance, circuit density, body composition consolidation | 5 |

---

---

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION (Weeks 1–4)

## Phase 1 Goals
Establish movement patterns, build connective tissue tolerance, introduce the client to consistent training stimulus, and stabilise blood glucose responses to exercise. Fat loss in this phase is modest but metabolic adaptation begins immediately.

## Phase 1 Training Structure
**4 sessions per week:** 2 full-body resistance sessions, 1 dedicated cardiovascular session, 1 active mobility/low-intensity session.

**Session duration:** 45–55 minutes.

---

### Week 1

**Session 1 — Full Body Resistance (Monday)**

Begin with a 5-minute warm-up on the treadmill or bike at a comfortable pace, followed by dynamic mobility: leg swings, hip circles, arm circles, and bodyweight squats (10 reps each). The purpose of the warm-up is not only muscular preparation but also to begin lowering blood glucose gently before the main session load.

*Main Work:*

- **Goblet Squat** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Use a light-to-moderate dumbbell (start with 6–8 kg and adjust based on form). Rest 90 seconds between sets. Focus on depth, upright torso, and controlled descent.
- **Seated Cable Row** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Moderate weight, full retraction of scapulae at the end of each rep. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift (RDL)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Light weight initially (8–10 kg dumbbells). Hinge at the hip, soft knee, feel the hamstring stretch. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Chest Press (flat bench)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Controlled eccentric (3-second lowering). Rest 90 seconds.
- **Plank Hold** — 3 sets × 20–30 seconds. Rest 60 seconds. Modify to knees if needed.
- **Banded Glute Bridge** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Light resistance band above knees. Rest 60 seconds.

Cool-down: 5 minutes of static stretching — hip flexors, hamstrings, chest, and thoracic rotation.

**Session 2 — Cardiovascular (Wednesday)**

**Moderate-Intensity Steady-State (MISS) Cardio — 30 minutes.**

Use the treadmill, stationary bike, or elliptical. Target heart rate zone: 50–65% of maximum heart rate (estimated max HR = 220 − 45 = 175 bpm; target zone = 88–114 bpm). This intensity is sufficient to improve insulin sensitivity and cardiovascular fitness without excessive stress. The client should be able to hold a conversation throughout. Check blood glucose before starting. If below 5.5 mmol/L, have a small 15g carbohydrate snack (e.g., a small banana) and wait 15 minutes before beginning.

**Session 3 — Full Body Resistance (Thursday)**

Warm-up as per Session 1.

*Main Work:*

- **Leg Press (machine)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Moderate load, feet shoulder-width, full range of motion. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Lat Pulldown (cable, wide grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Pull to upper chest, controlled return. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Shoulder Press (seated)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Neutral or pronated grip. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Reverse Lunge** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Bodyweight or very light dumbbells. Focus on balance and knee tracking. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Cable Tricep Pushdown** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Light weight, full extension. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Bicep Curl** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Controlled tempo. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Dead Bug** — 3 sets × 8 reps each side. Slow and controlled, lower back pressed to floor. Rest 60 seconds.

Cool-down: 5 minutes static stretching.

**Session 4 — Active Mobility & Low-Intensity (Saturday)**

This session serves recovery, parasympathetic nervous system activation, and blood glucose management. Research consistently shows that even low-intensity movement improves insulin sensitivity in the 24–48 hours following resistance training.

- 20-minute brisk walk (outdoors or treadmill, conversational pace)
- Yoga-style floor mobility sequence: cat-cow (2 × 10), child's pose (hold 60 seconds), pigeon pose each side (hold 45 seconds), supine spinal twist each side (hold 45 seconds), seated hamstring stretch (hold 45 seconds each side)
- Foam rolling: quads, IT band, thoracic spine, calves — 60–90 seconds per area

Total time: approximately 40 minutes.

---

### Weeks 2, 3, and 4 — Phase 1 Progression

The session structure remains identical across Weeks 1–4. Progression is applied as follows:

**Week 2:** Increase all resistance exercise loads by approximately 5% where form was solid in Week 1. Add 5 seconds to plank holds. Increase MISS cardio to 35 minutes.

**Week 3:** Introduce a fourth set on the primary compound movements (Goblet Squat, RDL, Leg Press, Lat Pulldown). Reduce rest periods on accessory exercises from 90 seconds to 75 seconds. MISS cardio remains at 35 minutes but increase pace slightly to keep heart rate in the upper end of the target zone (105–114 bpm).

**Week 4:** This is a **deload week**. Reduce volume by approximately 30% — drop back to 3 sets on all exercises, reduce loads by 10%, and shorten the cardio session to 25 minutes. This allows connective tissue recovery, hormonal reset, and prepares the body for the increased demands of Phase 2. Do not skip the deload — for a 45-year-old client with a metabolic condition, recovery is as important as the training stimulus itself.

---

---

# PHASE 2 — DEVELOPMENT (Weeks 5–8)

## Phase 2 Goals
Increase training frequency to five days per week, introduce upper/lower body splits, add metabolic conditioning work, and begin meaningful progressive overload. By this phase the client should have established movement competency and her body will be adapting to the training stimulus. Fat loss should become more visible and blood glucose responses to exercise should be more predictable.

## Phase 2 Training Structure
**5 sessions per week:** 2 upper body resistance sessions, 2 lower body resistance sessions, 1 metabolic conditioning session.

**Session duration:** 50–60 minutes.

---

### Week 5

**Session 1 — Upper Body (Monday)**

Warm-up: 5 minutes light cardio + band pull-aparts (2 × 15), shoulder circles, thoracic rotations.

*Main Work:*

- **Barbell or Dumbbell Bench Press** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Moderate-to-heavy load. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Bent-Over Dumbbell Row** — 4 sets × 10 reps each arm. Controlled, full range. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Cable Face Pull** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Light weight, external rotation emphasis. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Incline Dumbbell Curl** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Overhead Tricep Extension (cable or dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

**Session 2 — Lower Body (Tuesday)**

Warm-up: 5 minutes bike + glute activation circuit (clamshells 2 × 15, banded walks 2 × 10 each direction, bodyweight squats 2 × 10).

*Main Work:*

- **Barbell Back Squat or Goblet Squat (progressed load)** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Rest 2 minutes. If back squat technique is not yet solid, continue with goblet squat at a heavier load.
- **Romanian Deadlift (barbell or dumbbells)** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Walking Lunges** — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Bodyweight or light dumbbells. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Leg Curl (machine)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Leg Extension (machine)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Standing Calf Raise** — 3 sets × 20 reps. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Cable Woodchop (anti-rotation core)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Rest 60 seconds.

**Session 3 — Metabolic Conditioning (Wednesday)**

This session replaces the pure MISS cardio of Phase 1 and introduces **interval-based work**, which has superior evidence for improving insulin sensitivity compared to steady-state cardio alone. Post-exercise glucose uptake is elevated for up to 24 hours following high-intensity interval work.

**Format: 35-minute session**

- 5-minute warm-up (light bike or treadmill walk)
- **Interval block:** 20 minutes of 40 seconds work / 20 seconds rest, cycling through the following four exercises continuously:
  - Rowing machine (moderate-high effort)
  - Battle ropes (if available) or fast-paced stationary bike
  - Box step-ups (moderate height, alternating legs)
  - Kettlebell swing (moderate weight, 12–16 kg)
- 10-minute cool-down walk + stretching

Monitor heart rate throughout. Target 70–80% max HR during work intervals (123–140 bpm). If the client feels dizzy, lightheaded, or unusually fatigued, stop immediately and check blood glucose.

**Session 4 — Upper Body (Thursday)**

Warm-up as per Session 1.

*Main Work:*

- **Incline Dumbbell Press** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Seated Cable Row (close grip)** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Lateral Raise (dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Light weight, controlled. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Hammer Curl** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Tricep Dips (assisted machine or bench)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Pallof Press (cable)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Rest 60 seconds.

**Session 5 — Lower Body (Saturday)**

Warm-up as per Session 2.

*Main Work:*

- **Trap Bar Deadlift or Conventional Deadlift** — 4 sets × 6–8 reps. This is the primary strength movement of the week. Rest 2 minutes. Introduce the trap bar deadlift if available — it is more accessible for clients still developing hip hinge mechanics.
- **Bulgarian Split Squat (dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Hip Thrust (barbell or dumbbell)** — 4 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Seated Leg Curl** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Goblet Squat (tempo: 3-second descent)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Plank with Shoulder Tap** — 3 sets × 10 taps each side. Rest 60 seconds.

---

### Weeks 6, 7, and 8 — Phase 2 Progression

**Week 6:** Increase loads by 5% on all primary compound movements where three or more sets were completed with good form. Add one additional set to the metabolic conditioning interval block (22 minutes total work).

**Week 7:** Introduce **supersets** on accessory exercises to increase training density and metabolic demand. For example, pair bicep curls with tricep pushdowns, and lateral raises with face pulls. This reduces rest time between accessory work and elevates heart rate, improving the metabolic conditioning effect of resistance sessions. Increase deadlift and squat loads by a further 5%.

**Week 8:** **Deload week.** Reduce volume by 30%, drop back to 3 sessions (one upper, one lower, one light cardio). This is the second deload of the programme and is critical before the intensification phase. Use this week to reassess movement quality, note any areas of tightness or discomfort, and review progress metrics (weight, measurements, energy levels, blood glucose logs).

---

---

# PHASE 3 — INTENSIFICATION (Weeks 9–12)

## Phase 3 Goals
Maximise fat loss through increased training density and volume, consolidate strength gains, and drive the most significant improvements in glycaemic control. By Week 9, the client should have a solid movement foundation, improved cardiovascular fitness, and meaningful changes in body composition. This phase introduces circuit-style training elements and higher-intensity conditioning.

## Phase 3 Training Structure
**5 sessions per week:** 2 full-body strength sessions, 1 strength-endurance circuit session, 1 HIIT/conditioning session, 1 active recovery session.

**Session duration:** 55–65 minutes.

---

### Week 9

**Session 1 — Full Body Strength (Monday)**

Warm-up: 5 minutes cardio + dynamic mobility sequence.

*Main Work (straight sets, heavier loads):*

- **Barbell Back Squat** — 4 sets × 6 reps. Heavy, controlled. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Barbell Romanian Deadlift** — 4 sets × 6 reps. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Dumbbell Bench Press** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Weighted Pull-Up (assisted) or Lat Pulldown** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Shoulder Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 75 seconds.
- **Farmer's Carry** — 3 sets × 30 metres. Moderate-heavy dumbbells. Rest 90 seconds. This is an excellent full-body metabolic exercise with strong evidence for improving insulin sensitivity.

**Session 2 — Strength-Endurance Circuit (Tuesday)**

This session uses a **circuit format** with minimal rest between exercises and 90 seconds rest between rounds. The combination of resistance and cardiovascular demand creates a powerful metabolic effect and sustained post-exercise glucose uptake.

**4 rounds of the following circuit (rest 90 seconds between rounds):**

1. Goblet Squat — 15 reps
2. Dumbbell Row (each arm) — 12 reps
3. Dumbbell RDL — 12 reps
4. Push-Up (or incline push-up) — 15 reps
5. Kettlebell Swing — 15 reps
6. Plank Hold — 30 seconds
7. Box Step-Up — 12 reps each leg

Total circuit time: approximately 35–40 minutes of work. Cool-down: 10 minutes stretching.

**Session 3 — HIIT Conditioning (Wednesday)**

**Format: 30-minute session**

- 5-minute warm-up
- **Tabata-style intervals:** 20 seconds maximum effort / 10 seconds rest × 8 rounds = 4 minutes per exercise. Complete 4 exercises with 2 minutes rest between each:
  - Stationary bike sprint
  - Rowing machine sprint
  - Battle ropes
  - Treadmill incline walk at fast pace (if sprinting is not appropriate)
- 5-minute cool-down

Note: Tabata-style training has strong evidence for improving VO2 max and insulin sensitivity. Monitor the client closely in the first session. If she finds the intensity too high, reduce to 15 seconds work / 15 seconds rest and build up.

**Session 4 — Full Body Strength (Thursday)**

*Main Work:*

- **Trap Bar Deadlift** — 4 sets × 5 reps. Heaviest loads of the programme. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Hip Thrust (barbell)** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Incline Dumbbell Press** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Cable Row (wide grip)** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Bulgarian Split Squat** — 3 sets × 8 reps each leg. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Pallof Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps each side. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Farmer's Carry** — 3 sets × 30 metres. Rest 90 seconds.

**Session 5 — Active Recovery (Saturday)**

- 25–30 minute brisk walk or light swim
- Full foam rolling sequence (15 minutes)
- Stretching: full body, 45–60 seconds per position
- Optional: 10 minutes of guided breathing or mindfulness practice — this is not trivial. Chronic stress elevates cortisol, which directly raises blood glucose. Stress management is a legitimate component of glycaemic control.

---

### Weeks 10, 11, and 12 — Phase 3 Progression

**Week 10:** Increase loads on all primary lifts by 5%. Add a fifth round to the strength-endurance circuit. Increase HIIT session to 35 minutes by adding one additional exercise to the Tabata block.

**Week 11:** This is the peak week of the programme. Loads should be at their highest. Introduce **drop sets** on one exercise per resistance session — for example, after the final set of barbell squats, immediately reduce the weight by 30% and perform as many reps as possible. This technique increases metabolic stress and muscle fibre recruitment without adding additional sets.

**Week 12:** **Final assessment week.** Reduce volume by 20% but maintain intensity (loads stay the same, reduce sets by one per exercise). Use this week to conduct final measurements, reassess movement quality, and review blood glucose logs. The client should have a follow-up appointment with her diabetes care team to review HbA1c — meaningful reductions are realistic within 12 weeks of consistent exercise and dietary adherence.

---

---

# NUTRITION PLAN

## Nutritional Philosophy for Type 2 Diabetes and Fat Loss

The nutrition plan is built around four principles specific to this client's needs:

1. **Carbohydrate quality and timing over restriction** — total carbohydrate elimination is not necessary or sustainable. The goal is to choose low-glycaemic index (GI) carbohydrates, time them strategically around training, and avoid large carbohydrate loads in isolation.
2. **Protein prioritisation** — high protein intake preserves lean muscle mass during a caloric deficit, supports satiety, and has a minimal effect on blood glucose.
3. **Caloric deficit for fat loss** — a moderate deficit of 400–500 kcal per day is recommended. This is sufficient for meaningful fat loss (approximately 0.4–0.5 kg per week) without triggering excessive hunger, muscle loss, or metabolic adaptation.
4. **Meal structure to blunt glucose spikes** — eating patterns, food combinations, and meal timing all influence post-meal glucose responses.

---

## Estimated Caloric Targets

These are starting estimates and should be adjusted based on the client's response over the first two to three weeks. A registered dietitian referral is strongly recommended given the diabetic context.

- **Estimated Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE):** approximately 2,000–2,200 kcal/day for a moderately active 45-year-old woman (adjust based on actual body weight and activity level).
- **Target intake:** 1,550–1,700 kcal/day (creating a 400–500 kcal deficit).
- **Macronutrient split:**
  - **Protein:** 1.6–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight. For a 75 kg client, this is approximately 120–150 g protein per day. Protein has minimal impact on blood glucose and is the most important macronutrient for this client.
  - **Carbohydrates:** 35–40% of total calories, approximately 135–170 g per day, prioritising low-GI sources and timing the majority around training sessions.
  - **Fats:** 25–30% of total calories, approximately 45–55 g per day, emphasising unsaturated fats.

---

## Carbohydrate Guidelines

**Recommended carbohydrate sources (low-GI, high-fibre):**
Oats, sweet potato, quinoa, lentils, chickpeas, black beans, brown rice (in moderation), wholegrain bread, barley, most vegetables, berries, apples, and pears.

**Carbohydrates to minimise:**
White bread, white rice, white pasta, sugary cereals, fruit juice, soft drinks, sweets, cakes, biscuits, and processed snack foods. These cause rapid blood glucose spikes and are counterproductive to both glycaemic control and fat loss.

**Carbohydrate timing strategy:**
- The largest carbohydrate portion of the day should be consumed in the meal immediately following a training session. Post-exercise, muscle glucose transporters (GLUT4) are upregulated, meaning glucose is taken up by muscle

# Important Clinical Advisory — Fasted Morning Cardio for This Client

---

Before incorporating fasted cardio into this client's programme, I need to flag several significant concerns specific to her profile that you as her trainer should carefully consider and discuss with her medical team.

---

## Why Fasted Cardio Requires Caution Here

### 1. Metformin and Morning Physiology

Metformin is typically taken with meals, partly because it can cause nausea and gastrointestinal distress on an empty stomach. More relevantly for exercise, **the dawn phenomenon** is well-documented in type 2 diabetics — cortisol and growth hormone rise in the early morning hours, causing the liver to release glucose and pushing fasting blood glucose higher than it was at midnight. This means her morning fasting blood glucose may already be elevated before she begins exercise.

Performing cardio in this state is not inherently dangerous, but it means **she will not be starting from a stable metabolic baseline**, and the cortisol spike from exercise layered on top of the dawn phenomenon cortisol rise can cause a paradoxical **further rise in blood glucose** during and immediately after fasted cardio — particularly with higher-intensity efforts. This is the opposite of what we are trying to achieve.

### 2. Hypoglycaemia Risk Is Low But Not Zero

Metformin alone has a low hypoglycaemia risk. However, if the client has any other medications, supplements, or dietary patterns that affect insulin sensitivity, fasted exercise could push glucose lower than expected. At HbA1c 7.2%, her average blood glucose is running around 8.0–8.5 mmol/L, so severe hypoglycaemia is unlikely — but **sub-5.0 mmol/L readings before fasted exercise should be an absolute stop point.**

### 3. Cortisol and Muscle Catabolism

For a 45-year-old woman in a caloric deficit, fasted cardio adds a third cortisol stressor on top of caloric restriction and resistance training. Chronically elevated cortisol in this context can **accelerate muscle protein breakdown**, which is counterproductive to the insulin sensitivity improvements we are building through resistance training. This is particularly relevant for perimenopausal women, where oestrogen decline already reduces the anabolic signalling that protects muscle mass.

### 4. The Evidence Base Is Weaker Than Commonly Believed

The popular belief that fasted cardio burns significantly more fat than fed cardio is not well-supported in the literature when **total daily energy balance** is accounted for. Studies comparing fasted versus fed cardio over multiple weeks show no meaningful difference in fat loss outcomes when calories are matched. For this client, **adherence, blood glucose stability, and muscle preservation are more important variables than the marginal theoretical fat oxidation advantage of fasted training.**

---

## Recommendation

Rather than blanket fasted morning cardio, the following **modified fasted cardio protocol** is recommended. It captures the scheduling convenience and some of the metabolic benefits while managing the specific risks for a type 2 diabetic on Metformin.

---

# Modified Fasted Morning Cardio Protocol

## Non-Negotiable Pre-Session Checklist

Every single morning cardio session must begin with the following steps. These are not optional — make this a written routine the client follows independently on days you are not present.

**Step 1 — Blood glucose check upon waking.** The client must check her blood glucose before doing anything else, including coffee.

**Step 2 — Apply the traffic light system:**

| Blood Glucose Reading | Action |
|---|---|
| Below 5.0 mmol/L | **Do not exercise.** Consume 15–20g fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g., small glass of orange juice or 3–4 glucose tablets). Recheck in 15 minutes. Only proceed if reading rises above 5.5 mmol/L. |
| 5.0–5.5 mmol/L | Consume a small 10–15g carbohydrate snack (e.g., half a banana or a few oatcakes). Wait 10 minutes. Proceed with **low-intensity only** (walking, light cycling). |
| 5.6–10.0 mmol/L | **Green light.** Proceed with the planned session as described below. |
| Above 10.0 mmol/L | Proceed with **low-intensity only.** High blood glucose before exercise combined with exercise-induced cortisol can push glucose higher still. Do not perform intervals or high-intensity work in this state. |
| Above 14.0 mmol/L | **Do not exercise.** Contact GP or diabetes nurse. This reading suggests poor overnight control and requires medical review before exercise. |

**Step 3 — Have fast-acting glucose accessible during the session** (glucose tablets, small juice carton). Even on Metformin, this is good practice.

**Step 4 — Check blood glucose immediately post-session** and log it alongside the pre-session reading. This log is invaluable data — after four to six weeks, clear patterns will emerge showing how her body responds to morning exercise, and the programme can be refined accordingly.

---

## Intensity Guidelines for Fasted Morning Cardio

Given the physiological considerations above, fasted morning cardio for this client should be **predominantly low-to-moderate intensity.** This is the intensity range at which:

- Fat oxidation is genuinely maximised (not high intensity, contrary to popular belief)
- Cortisol response is minimised
- The risk of paradoxical blood glucose rise is lowest
- Muscle catabolism risk is lowest

**Target heart rate for fasted morning sessions: 50–65% of maximum heart rate (88–114 bpm).**

This is a brisk walk, a comfortable cycle, or a light elliptical pace — not a run, not intervals, not anything that causes breathlessness. Save higher-intensity work for fed, post-meal sessions later in the day or on gym days.

## Nutrition Adjustments for Fasted Morning Cardio

The addition of fasted morning sessions requires specific nutritional adjustments to protect muscle mass, support recovery, and manage blood glucose across the day.

### Immediately Post-Fasted Session

Within 30 minutes of completing the morning cardio session, the client must consume a **protein-led breakfast with a moderate low-GI carbohydrate component.** This is non-negotiable. Skipping breakfast after fasted cardio in a caloric deficit will accelerate muscle catabolism and is particularly harmful for a perimenopausal woman.

**Target post-fasted session breakfast:**
- 30–40g protein
- 30–40g low-GI carbohydrate
- Minimal fat in this meal (fat slows gastric emptying and delays glucose delivery to recovering muscles)

**Example breakfasts:**
- Greek yoghurt (full-fat, 200g) with mixed berries and a tablespoon of oats, plus 2 boiled eggs
- Scrambled eggs (3 whole eggs) on one slice of wholegrain toast with a small portion of smoked salmon
- Protein shake (whey or pea protein, 30g) blended with half a banana and 150ml skimmed milk, alongside a small bowl of porridge made with water

### On Double-Day Sessions (Morning Cardio + Afternoon Gym)

The meal between the morning fasted session and the afternoon gym session is critical. It must contain:
- 35–45g protein
- 50–60g low-GI carbohydrate (this is the largest carbohydrate meal of the day on these days, timed to fuel the afternoon session)
- Moderate healthy fat (10–15g)

**Example mid-day meal:**
- Grilled chicken breast (150g) with a medium sweet potato and a large green salad with olive oil dressing
- Tinned salmon with brown rice (150g cooked) and steamed broccoli and green beans

### Hydration for Fasted Sessions

The client should drink 500ml of water upon waking before the session and continue hydrating throughout. Dehydration impairs glucose regulation and cardiovascular performance. Plain black coffee is acceptable before fasted cardio — caffeine has been shown to improve fat oxidation and does not significantly affect blood glucose at moderate doses (one cup). However, if she notices elevated post-session blood glucose on days she has coffee versus days she does not, she should eliminate it from the pre-session routine, as caffeine can increase cortisol and hepatic glucose output in some individuals.

---

## Monitoring and Red Flags

Given the addition of fasted morning sessions, the following monitoring protocol should be in place throughout the 12 weeks:

**Daily logging (client self-monitors):**
- Fasting blood glucose upon waking
- Pre-session blood glucose
- Post-session blood glucose
- Energy levels (1–10 scale)
- Sleep quality (1–10 scale)
- Any symptoms of dizziness, unusual fatigue, or heart palpitations

**Trainer review:** Review the blood glucose log at every session. Look for trends — if fasted morning sessions are consistently associated with blood glucose rising above 10 mmol/L post-exercise, reduce intensity further or shift those sessions to post-breakfast. If readings are consistently stable and trending downward over weeks, this is a positive sign of improving insulin sensitivity.

**Medical review:** Ensure the client's GP or diabetes nurse is aware that fasted morning cardio has been added to her programme. At the 6-week mark, a blood glucose review with her medical team is advisable. If HbA1c is retested at 12 weeks, meaningful improvement from 7.2% is a realistic and motivating target.

---

## Summary of Key Rules for Fasted Morning Cardio

To consolidate everything above into a clear reference for both you and your client:

- **Always check blood glucose before starting.** No exceptions.
- **Never perform high-intensity fasted cardio.** Keep it at 50–65% max HR, with very limited moderate-intensity intervals only in Phase 3 and only when blood glucose logs support it.
- **Always eat within 30 minutes of finishing.** Protein-led, moderate low-GI carbohydrate breakfast every time.
- **On double-day training days, separate sessions by at least four hours** and eat a proper meal between them.
- **Log everything.** Blood glucose, energy, symptoms. This data protects the client and informs programme adjustments.
- **If in doubt, walk.** A brisk walk is never the wrong answer for this client in a fasted state.

- **Replenish liver glycogen** modestly without causing a large blood glucose spike
- **Stabilise blood glucose** after the cortisol-driven fluctuations of fasted exercise

- **Be practical and quick to prepare** — this is a morning meal after exercise, not a cooking project

### Meal 1 — Greek Yoghurt Protein Bowl

- 80g mixed berries (blueberries, raspberries, strawberries — all low GI)
- 1 tablespoon of ground flaxseed
- Small drizzle of honey (optional — only if blood glucose was on the lower end post-session, i.e., below 6.0 mmol/L)

**Approximate macros:** 38g protein / 22g carbohydrate / 10g fat / 330 kcal

**Why it works for her:** Greek yoghurt has a very low glycaemic index despite containing carbohydrate — the protein and fat matrix slows glucose absorption significantly. Berries are among the lowest-GI fruits available and are rich in polyphenols, which have independent evidence for improving insulin sensitivity. Flaxseed adds omega-3 fatty acids and soluble fibre, both of which support glycaemic control. **Preparation time:** 3 minutes. Can be partially prepped the night before by portioning the yoghurt and berries into a container.

**Ingredients:**
- 3 whole eggs, scrambled in a small amount of olive oil or cooking spray
- 75g smoked salmon
- 1 slice of rye bread (rye has a significantly lower GI than wholegrain wheat bread — GI approximately 45–50 versus 70+ for white bread)
- Handful of spinach or rocket on the side
- Black pepper, lemon juice

**Why it works for her:** Eggs are one of the most satiating foods per calorie and have essentially zero impact on blood glucose. Rye bread provides a slow-release carbohydrate that will sustain energy through the morning without a glucose spike. # Option B — Small Pre-Workout Meal Before Morning Cardio (Fed Session)

If you decide to move away from true fasted cardio and instead have her eat something small before the morning session, here is what that should look like.

## Principles for a Pre-Workout Meal in a Type 2 Diabetic

The pre-workout meal for this client must achieve something that is slightly paradoxical: it needs to **provide enough fuel to support the session** without **raising blood glucose so high that exercise becomes counterproductive.** The key is keeping the carbohydrate content modest, pairing it with protein, and avoiding high-GI foods entirely.

**Timing:** 45–60 minutes before the session. This allows partial digestion and glucose availability without the full post-meal glucose spike occurring during exercise.

**Macronutrient targets for pre-workout meal:**

| Macronutrient | Target |
|---|---|
| Protein | 15–20g |
| Carbohydrate | 15–25g low-GI only |
| Fat | Keep low (under 8g) — fat slows gastric emptying and may cause discomfort during cardio |
| Total calories | 150–220 kcal |

This is a **small, purposeful snack** — not a full meal. A full meal before morning cardio will cause digestive discomfort, a significant glucose spike, and will undermine the fat oxidation benefits of morning exercise entirely.

---

## Pre-Workout Snack Options

---

### Snack 1 — The Most Recommended Option: Plain Greek Yoghurt with Berries

**Ingredients:**
- 150g plain Greek yoghurt (full-fat or low-fat)
- 60g blueberries or raspberries

**Approximate macros:** 15g protein / 16g carbohydrate / 5g fat / 175 kcal

**Why it is the top recommendation:** This combination has the lowest glycaemic impact of all the options below. The protein and fat in the yoghurt significantly blunt the glucose response from the berries. It is light enough not to cause digestive discomfort during cardio. It is quick to prepare. And the protein content is sufficient to reduce muscle protein breakdown during the session without being so high that it diverts blood flow to digestion during exercise.

---

### Snack 2 — Hard-Boiled Egg and Oatcakes

**Ingredients:**
- 2 hard-boiled eggs (prepared the night before)
- 2 oatcakes (plain, no added sugar)

**Approximate macros:** 14g protein / 18g carbohydrate / 11g fat / 230 kcal

**Why it works:** Eggs provide fast, convenient protein with no blood glucose impact. Oatcakes have a low GI (approximately 55) and provide a small, slow-release carbohydrate source. The fat content is slightly higher than ideal for a pre-cardio snack but comes from beneficial egg yolk sources. Best suited to Phase 1 and 2 when session intensity is lower.

---

### Snack 3 — Small Portion of Overnight Oats

**Ingredients:**
- 25g rolled oats prepared with 100ml unsweetened almond milk overnight
- 1 tablespoon of plain Greek yoghurt stirred in
- Small sprinkle of cinnamon

**Approximate macros:** 8g protein / 22g carbohydrate / 4g fat / 165 kcal

**Why it works:** The protein content here is lower than ideal, making this the weakest option for muscle protection. However it is extremely easy to prepare, very gentle on the digestive system, and the slow-release carbohydrate from oats provides sustained energy for longer morning sessions. If using this option, consider adding a small amount of protein powder (10g) to bring the protein content up.

---

### Snack 4 — Rice Cake with Almond Butter and a Few Slices of Banana

**Ingredients:**
- 2 plain rice cakes
- 1 tablespoon natural almond butter (no added sugar)
- Half a small banana (approximately 50g)

**Approximate macros:** 6g protein / 26g carbohydrate / 8g fat / 210 kcal

**Important caveat:** This option has the highest GI of the four, primarily because rice cakes have a high GI (approximately 82) and banana is moderate-GI. The almond butter partially mitigates this, but this snack may cause a more noticeable glucose rise than the others. It is best reserved for Phase 3 when session intensity is highest and she needs more readily available fuel. **Check blood glucose 45 minutes after consuming this and before starting the session** to ensure it has not risen above 10 mmol/L.

---

## What to Avoid Entirely Before Morning Cardio

Regardless of whether she is doing fasted or fed morning cardio, the following should never be consumed in the pre-session window:

- **Fruit juice** — even fresh-squeezed. Extremely high GI, no fibre, rapid glucose spike.
- **Toast with jam or honey** — high GI carbohydrate with minimal protein to buffer the response.
- **Sugary cereals or granola** — marketed as healthy but typically high GI and high sugar.
- **Sports drinks or energy drinks** — entirely inappropriate for this client in any context.
- **Flavoured yoghurts** — most contain 15–25g of added sugar per serving.
- **Protein bars** — most commercial protein bars contain significant added sugar and highly processed carbohydrates. If she uses one, check the label carefully: look for under 10g sugar, over 15g protein, and recognisable ingredients.

| True fasted cardio — post-session meal | Meal 1 (Greek Yoghurt Protein Bowl) or Meal 2 (Eggs and Smoked Salmon on Rye) |
| Time-pressed post-session | Meal 5 (Protein Smoothie) |
| Double-day training (morning cardio + afternoon gym) | Meal 3 (Protein Oats) for higher carbohydrate fuel |
| Moving to fed morning cardio — pre-session snack | Snack 1 (Greek Yoghurt and Berries) as first choice |
| Higher intensity Phase 3 fed sessions | Snack 2 (Eggs and Oatcakes) |
